title: From the Archive: How the Past Shadows China’s Future
gist: Historian Odd Arne Westad tells Dan Kurtz-Phelan that the Cold War is the wrong template for U.S.-China rivalry — the pre-1914 multipolar era is the better guide — and argues Taiwan is the most likely trigger for great-power war, warning that a recently retired Chinese general told him Beijing believes its window to reunify Taiwan by force is closing.

themes.theme: Multipolarity replaces the Cold War framing

insights.claim: The Cold War is a faulty and potentially dangerous analogy for the U.S.-China relationship because China's leadership sees the world as multipolar rather than bipolar, and because, unlike the self-isolated Soviet Union, both the U.S. and China compete within the same integrated global economic system.
insights.speaker: Odd Arne Westad
insights.so_what: Investors relying on Cold War-style containment frameworks to model U.S.-China decoupling risk are using the wrong template, per Westad — economic entanglement makes clean separation far harder than it was with the USSR.
insights.quote: the Cold War parallel—more used, I think, back then than what it is now—is still a faulty, and, to some extent, dangerous analogy to use for the Sino-American relationship now
insights.locator: I think, going back to that 2019 article

insights.claim: Because the great powers of today compete within the same international economic system rather than one side self-isolating as the Soviet Union did, Sino-American competition is structurally harder to manage than the Cold War — more parties are involved and the links between economic strategy and other forms of state power are far murkier.
insights.speaker: Odd Arne Westad
insights.so_what: Explains why trade, tech, and security policy toward China can't be cleanly separated the way Cold War-era containment separated East from West — a caution against expecting simple decoupling.
insights.locator: Also, crucially, because this is really important

insights.claim: True global multipolarity of the kind now emerging hasn't existed since before 1914, making the pre-World War I era, not the Cold War, the more relevant historical parallel for understanding today's great-power dynamics.
insights.speaker: Odd Arne Westad
insights.so_what: Sets the frame for the interview's central warning: pre-1914 multipolar instability, not Cold War bipolar stability, is the operative historical risk model for today.
insights.locator: But together these time periods have lasted

insights.claim: Chinese strategy is straightforward at the regional level: Beijing wants to become the predominant power in East Asia and the western Pacific, but Westad sees little evidence of a deliberate, specific Chinese strategy to become globally dominant and replace the United States.
insights.speaker: Odd Arne Westad
insights.so_what: Pushes back on maximalist 'China wants global hegemony' framing — useful for calibrating how far to extrapolate China-risk premia beyond the East Asia/western Pacific theater.
insights.locator: So if you think in international terms

insights.claim: Westad warns that great-power appetite can grow with eating — the absence of a current Chinese strategy for global domination doesn't mean China wouldn't pursue it given the opportunity, and dominating East Asia already means dominating what will be the world's most consequential economic and technological region.
insights.speaker: Odd Arne Westad
insights.so_what: A caveat against complacency: regional Chinese dominance is not a lesser or contained outcome, given the region's economic weight.
insights.locator: The first one is, of course, as we see from the twentieth century

insights.claim: Over the past two decades China's strategic aims have shown consistency, but analysts including Westad significantly underestimated the speed of China's capability growth, especially its military transformation and its innovation capacity, which he says the analyst community got 'entirely wrong as late as half a decade ago.'
insights.speaker: Odd Arne Westad
insights.so_what: A direct admission of past forecasting error on China's innovation and military pace — a caution against anchoring current China forecasts on the same conservative assumptions.
insights.locator: I’m thinking about the growth of Chinese technological capabilities

insights.claim: Westad downplays Xi Jinping's personal influence on China's strategic trajectory, arguing that when tested, Xi has chosen directions broadly consistent with his predecessors — the key difference is that China now has far more relative power than any predecessor's China did.
insights.speaker: Odd Arne Westad
insights.so_what: Suggests China-strategy continuity would likely outlast a Xi leadership transition, tempering 'personalist regime risk' framing of China policy.
insights.locator: I think we are, to some extent, overfocusing

themes.theme: Xi's use of history and legitimacy

insights.claim: Westad compares Xi Jinping less to Mao Zedong than to Qing-era emperors Kangxi and Qianlong, arguing the shared historical lesson is that growing power makes managing regional relationships harder, not easier, since neighbors resist subservience even as they nominally defer to the dominant power.
insights.speaker: Odd Arne Westad
insights.so_what: Implies China's growing power will generate more, not less, regional friction with neighbors — relevant to South China Sea, Korea, and broader East Asian tension forecasts.
insights.locator: So I think Xi has a lot in common

insights.claim: Xi Jinping is unusually preoccupied — more than any CCP leader including Mao — with presenting his rule as the fulfillment of a long arc of Chinese imperial history, reviving an extended 'century of humiliation' narrative and directly connecting CCP legitimacy to a reimagined ancient, predominant China.
insights.speaker: Odd Arne Westad
insights.so_what: Signals that Xi's domestic legitimacy is now tied to restoring China's historical regional predominance, raising the political cost of any perceived retreat on core sovereignty issues like Taiwan.
insights.locator: This is actually one of the things that is interesting

themes.theme: The pre-WWI parallel and Taiwan as the flashpoint

insights.claim: Westad's central warning, from his book The Coming Storm and essay 'Sleepwalking Toward War,' is that today's structural conditions — a receding hegemonic anchor power (Britain then, the U.S. now), fraying globalization, and rising nationalism — closely resemble the pre-1914 period more than the Cold War or 1930s analogies typically invoked.
insights.speaker: Odd Arne Westad
insights.so_what: Frames the current period as structurally closer to a pre-WWI great-power crisis risk than a stable Cold War-style standoff — a higher baseline risk assumption for great-power conflict.
insights.locator: I think there are many reasons for this, Dan

insights.claim: Westad draws a direct China-Germany parallel: like Wilhelmine Germany, China is a rapidly rising power whose established rivals have mostly responded to its rise by demanding it stop growing rather than finding it a role in the international system — citing historian Paul Kennedy's description of Britain telling Germany, 'Little Hans, if you stop growing everything will be okay.'
insights.speaker: Odd Arne Westad
insights.so_what: Suggests that Western policy focused solely on constraining China's growth, without offering it a legitimate role in global governance, echoes a historical pattern that failed to prevent war.
insights.quote: Little Hans, if you stop growing everything will be okay.
insights.locator: as my colleague Paul Kennedy wrote in his wonderful book

insights.claim: Westad sees a mirrored problem on the U.S. side of the parallel: the speed with which the United States, especially under the second Trump administration, has moved to undermine the international system it built echoes how quickly Britain was willing to unwind the free-trade order it had anchored before 1914.
insights.speaker: Odd Arne Westad
insights.so_what: Places responsibility for rising great-power risk on both sides, not just China's rise — relevant to assessing how U.S. retreat from multilateral institutions itself elevates conflict risk.
insights.locator: Maybe first and foremost, the speed with which

insights.claim: Westad calls Taiwan 'a little bit like Alsace, Bosnia, and Belgium rolled into one' — nationally symbolic territory that cannot be bargained away (Alsace), a likely flashpoint (Bosnia), and the test of whether a great-power military move triggers outside intervention (Belgium) — with China's core calculation mirroring Germany's 1914 calculus about whether the dominant naval power (Britain then, the U.S. now) would intervene.
insights.speaker: Odd Arne Westad
insights.so_what: A precise historical framework for how Beijing may be weighing a Taiwan operation — the decisive variable, per Westad, is whether China believes the U.S. and allies would intervene.
insights.quote: Taiwan is a little bit like Alsace, Bosnia, and Belgium rolled into one.
insights.locator: So Taiwan is, if you want to use the parallel

insights.claim: A recently retired Chinese general told Westad directly that Beijing believes it has a closing window to achieve Taiwan reunification, because generational identity shifts among younger Taiwanese who feel 'much less Chinese' than their parents' or grandparents' generation could make reunification impossible 'even if we used all the military force in the world.'
insights.speaker: Odd Arne Westad
insights.so_what: First-hand testimony from a Chinese military insider suggesting a 'use it or lose it' logic on Taiwan timing — a high-signal input for anyone modeling Taiwan Strait conflict probability and timing.
insights.quote: If we do not act towards reunification before it is impossible to carry out for reasons that have to do with identity and general sentiment within the island, then we wouldn’t be able to make this happen
insights.locator: I had one recently retired general pull me aside

insights.claim: A second driver of Chinese urgency on Taiwan, which Westad hears 'fairly often' in Beijing policy circles though he calls it a weak argument, is the belief that a China unable to reunify its own territory can never achieve the regional predominance long central to Chinese strategy.
insights.speaker: Odd Arne Westad
insights.so_what: A second, distinct psychological/strategic driver (beyond the closing-identity-window argument) pushing Beijing toward earlier rather than later action on Taiwan.
insights.locator: The other issue, I think, is connected to CCP perceptions

insights.claim: Westad draws his sharpest 1914 warning from German thinking that war might be better sooner than later given signs of domestic economic stress and fear that rivals, especially Russia, were strengthening — and says he hears an analogous 'act now before the window closes' logic in some Chinese discussions of Taiwan today.
insights.speaker: Odd Arne Westad
insights.so_what: Directly flags a 'maximum moment' risk logic — the idea that perceived economic weakening could make Beijing more, not less, likely to act sooner on Taiwan — a key tail-risk scenario to monitor.
insights.locator: There was the fear that other powers were strengthening themselves

themes.theme: China-Russia alignment as a Sarajevo-style risk

insights.claim: Westad calls China's alignment with Russia a 'de facto alliance with a decrepit empire,' structurally analogous to Germany's WWI-era alliance with Austria-Hungary — the only ally available rather than the most desirable one — warning it could drag China into conflicts, such as those touching Russia-North Korea or Russia-Turkey frictions, that are not fundamentally China's own quarrels.
insights.speaker: Odd Arne Westad
insights.so_what: Identifies a specific entanglement risk channel — China could be pulled into a conflict it didn't choose via its Russia alignment, echoing how Austria-Hungary dragged Germany into World War I.
insights.locator: just like in that situation, China is moving closer

insights.claim: Westad says he is surprised by the speed and totality of Russia's economic subservience to China, calling it historically unprecedented for one great power to hand away so much economic advantage to a near neighbor even within a de facto alliance.
insights.speaker: Odd Arne Westad
insights.so_what: Highlights an unusually asymmetric power dynamic in the China-Russia relationship, useful context for assessing which side has more leverage in joint sanctions-evasion, energy, and arms deals.
insights.quote: I don’t think we have another example from history, at least I can’t think of one, where one great power so willingly hands away economic advantages to a near neighbor
insights.locator: Yes, I have, I mean, by the speed of it

insights.claim: Westad warns Russian arms and technology transfers to North Korea are a specifically dangerous flashpoint that could pull China into an unwanted Korean Peninsula crisis, and says Beijing is aware of the risk but constrained from voicing displeasure by its own deepening ties with Pyongyang.
insights.speaker: Odd Arne Westad
insights.so_what: Flags Russia-North Korea military cooperation as a specific escalation pathway on the Korean Peninsula that China cannot easily restrain, relevant to Korea-risk monitoring.
insights.locator: I also see Russian actions with regard to North Korea

insights.claim: Westad argues China's Russia alignment carries underpriced long-term costs, including having driven China's relationship with the European Union into what he calls a surprising 'freefall' over recent months.
insights.speaker: Odd Arne Westad
insights.so_what: Suggests China's EU relationship is deteriorating faster than expected as a direct consequence of its Russia ties — relevant to EU-China trade and investment policy forecasts.
insights.locator: It’s going to have a disastrous relationship

insights.claim: Westad rejects the near-term feasibility of a 'reverse Kissinger' strategy (the U.S. courting Russia to isolate China), arguing that any U.S. outreach to Moscow before the Ukraine war ends would simply reward and encourage Russia's current behavior.
insights.speaker: Odd Arne Westad
insights.so_what: Pushes back directly against a policy idea reportedly circulating in the Trump administration, arguing it would backfire rather than split Moscow from Beijing.
insights.locator: Do I think that there is a possibility at the moment

themes.theme: How Washington and Beijing see each other now

insights.claim: Westad reports growing fear rather than confidence on both sides: American anxiety about domestic political dysfunction and being technologically overtaken, and Chinese anxiety — voiced to him on his most recent Beijing trip — that the economic model driving China's rise is starting to weaken.
insights.speaker: Odd Arne Westad
insights.so_what: Both sides currently perceive relative decline rather than triumphalism, which Westad notes historically is not itself a war trigger but 'may play a role if the right crisis comes along.'
insights.locator: I’m not sure that’s true, Dan

insights.claim: Westad detects a genuine Trump-administration effort to reduce U.S.-China tension, which he views positively in principle, but says most Chinese policymakers (unlike parts of the Chinese public, who admire Trump as a decisive strong leader) see more danger than opportunity, because his administration's unpredictable decision-making is hard for Beijing to forecast.
insights.speaker: Odd Arne Westad
insights.so_what: Unpredictability, not hostility per se, is what worries Chinese policymakers most about the current U.S. administration — a factor that could raise miscalculation risk in a crisis.
insights.locator: So the idea that you find in this country

insights.claim: Westad's closing risk flag is that unpredictable U.S. crisis decision-making could lead Chinese leaders to erroneous conclusions about U.S. resolve in a crisis, echoing how the conflation of unrelated resentments, fears, and military doctrines across many issues helped produce the 1914 spiral into war.
insights.speaker: Odd Arne Westad
insights.so_what: The interview's bottom-line tail-risk warning: miscalculation driven by unpredictable U.S. signaling, not deliberate aggression by either side, is Westad's chief near-term concern for a great-power crisis.
insights.locator: That’s a danger. I mean, that could easily lead to conclusions
